The HSCT aircraft optimization problem was solved using three alternate approaches: the original FLOPS analyzer and two approximate (derived) analyzers based on neural network and linear regression approximation.
The approximate analyzers were calibrated and used in three different ranges of the design variables: narrow (interpolated), standard, and wide (extrapolated).
In the restricted range, a 1% deviation was observed in the optimum gross takeoff weight of the aircraft using the approximation methods.
In the standard and wide ranges, the deviation increased to 2% for the approximation methods.
The approximation-based optimization processes reduced the computing time from hours (for the FLOPS-based optimization) to minutes.
Calibrating the approximate analyzers required substantial computational time for both neural network and regression methods.
The HSCT aircraft problem had a baseline mission to carry 305 passengers 5000 nautical miles at a cruise speed of Mach 2.4.
The HSCT aircraft had four mixed-flow turbofan engines.
The research was conducted by researchers from NASA Lewis Research Center, NASA Langley Research Center, and the Ohio Aerospace Institute.
The paper builds on previous work presented in a 1997 publication by Patnaik et al.
The neural network and regression approximation concepts were found to be satisfactory for the analysis and design optimization of the HSCT aircraft problem.
The approximation methods were able to eliminate the instability issues experienced with the FLOPS analyzer.
Calibrating the approximate analyzers over a wider (standard) range and then using them to optimize over a narrower (restricted) range was the preferred approach.
The research aimed to alleviate the limitations of the earlier FLOPS-based optimization process, which included substantial computing time and instability at certain design points.
The use of approximation methods significantly reduced the computing time required for the optimization process.
